claim: A super-relaxed (SRX) state of myosin has been discovered in the last decade.
source: However, in the last decade, a new functional super-relaxed (SRX) state of myosin has been discovered
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the discovery timeframe of the SRX state.

claim: The SRX state has a 10-fold slower ATP turnover rate than the disordered relaxed (DRX) state.
source: which has a 10-fold slower ATP turnover rate than the already-known non-actin-bound, disordered relaxed (DRX) state
evidence: The abstract directly states the quantitative difference in ATP turnover rates between SRX and DRX states.

claim: The DRX and SRX states are in dynamic equilibrium under resting muscle conditions.
source: These two states are in dynamic equilibrium under resting muscle conditions
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes the relationship between the two states.

claim: The DRX↔SRX equilibrium is thought to be a significant contributor to adaptive thermogenesis in skeletal muscle.
source: are thought to be significant contributors to adaptive thermogenesis in skeletal muscle
evidence: The abstract presents this as a hypothesis about the physiological role of the equilibrium.

claim: The SRX state can act as a reserve pool that may be recruited when there is sustained demand for increased cardiac muscle power.
source: can act as a reserve pool that may be recruited when there is a sustained demand for increased cardiac muscle power
evidence: The abstract presents this as a potential functional role of the SRX state.

claim: Roger Cooke and colleagues discovered the super-relaxed (SRX) state of myosin in rabbit skeletal muscle fibers ten years ago.
source: Ten years ago, a seminal breakthrough was made when Roger Cooke and colleagues discovered a new functional state of myosin molecules in rabbit skeletal muscle fibers, which they termed the super-relaxed(SRX) state (Stewart et al., 2010).
evidence: The text explicitly attributes the discovery to Roger Cooke and colleagues with a citation.

claim: The SRX state has been confirmed in cardiac and skeletal fibers from many different species.
source: Multiple subsequent studies have confirmed this SRX state in cardiac and skeletal fibers from many different species (Hooijman et al., 2011; McNamara et al., 2015; Naber et al., 2011; Anderson et al., 2018).
evidence: The text cites multiple studies confirming the SRX state across species.

claim: The population of the SRX state is measured kinetically by following the release of fluorescent ATP hydrolysis products from myosin.
source: The population of the SRX state is measured kinetically by following the release of fluorescent ATP hydrolysis products from myosin.
evidence: The text explicitly describes the experimental method for measuring SRX state population.

claim: The SRX state has an ultra-slow release of ATP hydrolysis products relative to myosins in other states.
source: A hallmark of this SRX state is an ultra-slow release of the ATP hydrolysis products relative to myosins in other states.
evidence: The text explicitly defines a key characteristic of the SRX state.

claim: Myosin in muscle sarcomere exists in three different functional states.
source: In other words, in the muscle sarcomere, myosin is thought to exist in three different functional states (Figure 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states this and references Figure 1 for illustration.

claim: The active cycling state of myosin involves actin-activated ATP hydrolysis with a rapid ATP turnover time of <1 s.
source: The first is the active cycling state of myosin, which involves actin-activated ATP hydrolysis and a rapid ATP turnover time of <1 s.
evidence: The text explicitly describes the characteristics of the active cycling state.

claim: The DRX state is the ATP turnover state of myosin in the absence of actin with a very slow ATP turnover time of <30 s.
source: The second state, often called the disordered relaxed (DRX) state , is the ATP turnover state of myosin in the absence of actin, which has a very slow ATP turnover time of <30 s.
evidence: The text explicitly describes the characteristics of the DRX state.

claim: The SRX state has ATP turnover times of more than 100 s.
source: The third, or the SRX state, is the state that has even more prolonged ATP turnover times of more than 100 s.
evidence: The text explicitly provides the ATP turnover time for the SRX state.

claim: In skeletal and cardiac muscle fibers, 50–60% of the myosin heads are in the SRX state.
source: In skeletal and cardiac muscle fibers, it has been estimated that 50–60% of the myosin heads are in the SRX state and are hypothesized to not participate in contractility (Stewart et al., 2010; Hooijman et al., 2011).
evidence: The text cites studies that estimated the proportion of myosin heads in the SRX state.

claim: Myosins in the SRX state are hypothesized to not participate in contractility.
source: In skeletal and cardiac muscle fibers, it has been estimated that 50–60% of the myosin heads are in the SRX state and are hypothesized to not participate in contractility (Stewart et al., 2010; Hooijman et al., 2011).
evidence: The text presents this as a hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: The interacting-heads motif (IHM) is a folded-back structural state of myosin where the two S1 heads asymmetrically interact with one another and fold back onto the S2 tail.
source: Although there is no atomic-level structure of myosin in the SRX state, researchers have previously discovered a folded-back structural state of myosin, which is termed the interacting-heads motif (IHM), where the two myosin subfragment 1 (S1) heads of myosin asymmetrically interact with one another and fold back onto its subfragment 2 (S2) tail (Woodhead et al., 2005; Zoghbi et al., 2008; Wendt et al., 1999; Wendt et al., 2001; Burgess et al., 2007; Jung et al., 2008a; Jung et al., 2008b) (reviewed in Trivedi et al., 2018 and Alamo et al., 2018).
evidence: The text explicitly describes the IHM structure with multiple citations.

claim: The IHM state was discovered using cryo- and conventional electron microscopy in intact thick filaments and purified myosins.
source: This state was discovered using cryo- and conventional electron microscopy in intact thick filaments isolated from various types of muscle and purified myosins in solution.
evidence: The text explicitly describes the methods used to discover the IHM state.

claim: The first 3D structure of the folded-back conformation was reported in smooth muscle myosin by Wendt et al., 1999.
source: In fact, the first 3D structure of this folded-back conformation was reported in smooth muscle myosin by Wendt et al., 1999.
evidence: The text explicitly attributes the first 3D structure to a specific study.

claim: Many researchers hypothesize that the SRX state is related to the IHM state.
source: Many researchers have put forward an appealing hypothesis that the SRX state is related to this IHM state (Hooijman et al., 2011; Alamo et al., 2016; Cooke, 2011; Nogara et al., 2016a; Wilson et al., 2014)
evidence: The text explicitly states this hypothesis with supporting citations.

claim: Recent biochemical studies have shown that there are myosin states other than IHM that are SRX states.
source: However, many recent biochemical studies have shown that there are myosin states other than IHM that are SRX states (discussed below) (Figure 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 1.

claim: Phosphorylation of RLC depopulates the SRX state in rabbit skeletal muscle fibers.
source: The first study to report the ability of RLC phosphorylation to depopulate the myosin SRX state was in rabbit skeletal muscle fibers (Stewart et al., 2010) and subsequently reproduced in tarantula skeletal muscle (Naber et al., 2011).
evidence: The text cites studies demonstrating the effect of RLC phosphorylation on SRX state.

claim: A phosphomimetic version of the RLC (S15D) in HCM-causing R58Q RLC mutant background depopulated the SRX state in skinned porcine papillary muscle fibers.
source: A similar observation was made where a phosphomimetic version of the RLC, S15D, in HCM-causing R58Q RLC mutant background, depopulated the SRX state in skinned porcine papillary muscle fibers (Yadav et al., 2019).
evidence: The text cites a study showing the effect of phosphomimetic RLC on SRX state.

claim: Phosphorylation of RLC with MLCK or depletion of RLC decreases the myosin population in the SRX state in reconstituted full-length porcine cardiac myosin thick filaments.
source: In reconstituted full-length porcine cardiac myosin thick filaments, it has also been recently reported that either phosphorylation of the RLC with MLCK or depletion of RLC decreases the myosin population in the SRX state (Gollapudi et al., 2020a).
evidence: The text cites a study demonstrating the effect of RLC phosphorylation and depletion on SRX state.

claim: RLC phosphorylation-mediated shift in DRX↔SRX state equilibrium toward the DRX state has been correlated with the depopulation of the structural IHM state.
source: This shift towards the DRX state has been correlated with the depopulation of the structural IHM state upon RLC phosphorylation (Alamo et al., 2016).
evidence: The text cites a study correlating RLC phosphorylation effects with IHM state changes.

claim: The two RLCs bind to each other forming one of the major interfaces stabilizing the IHM state.
source: The observation that factors that affect the RLC also affect the population of the SRX state is not surprising if one assumes that the IHM state is a major source of the SRX state, as the two RLCs bind to each other forming one of the major interfaces stabilizing the IHM state (Alamo et al., 2016).
evidence: The text cites a study describing the RLC-RLC interface in the IHM state.

claim: Ca2+ binding to ELC in scallop regulatory domain regulates molluscan muscle contraction.
source: The role of essential light chain (ELC) and how Ca2+ binding to ELC (in the scallop regulatory domain containing two light chains together with a short fragment of the heavy chain) regulates molluscan muscle contraction has been the focus of study in the laboratories of Andrew Szent-Gyorgyi and others (Szent-Györgyi, 1975; Fromherz and Szent-Györgyi, 1995; Chantler, 2006; Trybus, 1994).
evidence: The text cites multiple studies on Ca2+ binding to ELC in molluscan muscle.

claim: Ca2+ binding to ELC enzymatically and structurally turns on myosin from its IHM-like 'off' state.
source: Ca2+ binding to ELC has been shown to enzymatically and structurally turn on the myosin from its IHM-like 'off' state (Woodhead et al., 2013).
evidence: The text cites a study demonstrating the effect of Ca2+ binding to ELC on myosin state.

claim: The N-terminal extension of ELC may play an essential role in regulating myosin motor function and force production in striated muscle.
source: Several laboratories have demonstrated that a specific N-terminal extension of the ELC may play an essential role in regulating myosin motor function and force production in striated muscle (Kazmierczak et al., 2009; Muthu et al., 2011; Guhathakurta et al., 2015).
evidence: The text cites multiple studies on the role of ELC N-terminal extension.

claim: Lack of the N-terminus of ELC in mice (Tg-Δ43) resulted in a significant increase in the population of myosin in the SRX state.
source: The lack of the N-terminus of the ELC in mice resulted in a significant increase in the population of myosin in the SRX state, hence decreasing the proportion of myosin heads that are available to interact with actin (Sitbon et al., 2020).
evidence: The text cites a study showing the effect of ELC N-terminus deletion on SRX state.

claim: Myosin purified from Tg-Δ43 hearts showed significantly decreased ATP utilization and low actin-activated myosin ATPase compared to WT hearts.
source: In agreement, myosin purified from Tg-Δ43 hearts showed significantly decreased ATP utilization and low actin-activated myosin ATPase compared to that from wild-type (WT) hearts.
evidence: The text describes experimental data comparing Tg-Δ43 and WT myosin.

claim: In relaxed skeletal muscle, approximately 50% of myosins remain in the SRX state and the remainder is in the DRX state.
source: In relaxed skeletal muscle, it has been estimated that ~50% of the myosins remain in the SRX state, and the remainder is in the DRX state (Stewart et al., 2010; Cooke, 2011).
evidence: The text cites studies estimating the proportion of myosins in different states.

claim: There is a progressive loss of muscle strength with aging, termed dynapenia, independent of muscle size or the presence of neurological or muscular diseases.
source: It is also known that independent of muscle size or the presence of neurological or muscular diseases, there is a progressive loss of muscle strength with aging, termed dynapenia.
evidence: The text states this as established knowledge about aging and muscle strength.

claim: Age-related impairment of skeletal muscle contractility is more prominent in post-menopausal women than in men of the same age group.
source: Such age-related impairment of skeletal muscle contractility is more prominent in post-menopausal women than in men of the same age group.
evidence: The text states this as known information about gender differences in aging.

claim: No significant effects on the SRX population were observed as a function of age or sex in psoas muscle of young and aged C57BL/6 mice.
source: This hypothesis was tested in the psoas muscle of young (3–4 months old) and aged (26–28 months old) C57BL/6 male and female mice, and no significant effects on the SRX population as a function of age or sex (Phung et al., 2018) were observed.
evidence: The text cites a study that found no age or sex effects on SRX population.

claim: For female mice only, the ATPase cycling time of myosin in both the DRX and SRX states was significantly faster with age.
source: However, only for female mice, the ATPase cycling time of myosin in both the DRX and SRX states was significantly faster with age.
evidence: The text describes a specific finding about female mice and aging.

claim: The ovarian hormone estradiol is the key hormonal signal to skeletal muscle in females, and its deficiency is detrimental to myosin and muscle function.
source: It is known that the ovarian hormone estradiol is the key hormonal signal to skeletal muscle in females, and its deficiency is detrimental to myosin and muscle function.
evidence: The text states this as established knowledge about estradiol's role.

claim: In ovariectomized C57BL/6 mice, the ATP turnover rate of the SRX population was significantly increased compared to non-operative controls.
source: In an earlier study (Colson et al., 2015) by the same laboratory, single turnover experiments in the ovariectomized C57BL/6 mice revealed two distinct populations of myosin in the SRX and DRX states in a similar proportion to the populations seen in the control mice. However, the ATP turnover rate of the SRX population was significantly increased compared to the non-operative controls.
evidence: The text cites a study showing the effect of ovariectomy on SRX state ATP turnover.

claim: Chronic treatment of ovariectomy mice with estradiol for 60 days reverted the effect on SRX ATP turnover rate to WT control levels.
source: This effect was reverted to the WT control by a 60 days chronic treatment of the ovariectomy mice with estradiol, but not by treatment of the isolated psoas muscle with estradiol, suggesting that estradiol-mediated signaling reversibly regulates slow ATP turnover by myosin.
evidence: The text describes experimental results showing estradiol's effect on SRX state.

claim: Ca2+ plays a significant role in the activation of skeletal and cardiac muscle contraction mediated by direct binding to the actin–tropomyosin–troponin regulated thin-filament complex.
source: Ca2+ plays a significant role in a variety of biological processes in the body. One such well-studied process is the activation of skeletal and cardiac muscle contraction mediated by direct binding of Ca2+ to the actin–tropomyosin–troponin regulated thin-filament complex (reviewed by Ebashi and Endo, 1968, and Gordon et al., 2000).
evidence: The text cites reviews describing Ca2+'s role in muscle contraction.

claim: Ca2+ binding to scallop myosin destabilizes the myosin from the IHM-like 'off' state.
source: As discussed earlier, Ca2+ binding to scallop myosin destabilizes the myosin from the IHM-like 'off' state, a mechanism that has not been evolutionarily propagated in the vertebrate system.
evidence: The text states this as a known mechanism in scallop myosin.

claim: The Ca2+ sensitivity of the rate of force development in vertebrate skeletal muscle is mediated in part by the RLC subunit of the myosin cross-bridge.
source: Some early work by the laboratories of Richard Moss and others has shown that the Ca2+ sensitivity of the rate of force development in vertebrate skeletal muscle is mediated in part by the RLC subunit of the myosin cross-bridge (Metzger et al., 1989; Metzger and Moss, 1992; Metzger and Moss, 1990; Metzger and Moss, 1991).
evidence: The text cites multiple studies on Ca2+ sensitivity and RLC.

claim: Ca2+ and not Mg2+ binding to reconstituted porcine cardiac myosin filaments depopulated the myosin SRX state.
source: It is only recently that a study has reported that Ca2+ and not Mg2+ binding to reconstituted porcine cardiac myosin filaments depopulated the myosin SRX state, thereby proposing Ca2+-mediated activation of the thick filament as an additional regulation of the vertebrate muscle (Sa et al., 2019).
evidence: The text cites a study showing Ca2+'s specific effect on SRX state.

claim: Fast skeletal muscle type has a lesser population of myosins in the SRX state than the slow muscle type.
source: It has recently been shown that the fast skeletal muscle type has a lesser population of myosins in the SRX state than the slow muscle type (Phung et al., 2020), suggesting higher energy consumption by the fast muscle types.
evidence: The text cites a study comparing SRX state populations in different muscle types.

claim: Approximately 60–70% of the ATP generated in cardiac muscle is thought to be utilized by myosins.
source: It has been guessed that ~60–70% of the ATP generated in the cardiac muscle is thought to be utilized by the myosins (Barclay, 2015).
evidence: The text cites an estimate of ATP utilization by myosins in cardiac muscle.

claim: In rabbit fast and slow skeletal muscle fibers, ADP binding to myosin results in a possible strain-mediated depopulation of the SRX state.
source: For example, in rabbit fast and slow skeletal muscle fibers, ADP binding to the myosin attaches the myosin motor strongly to actin and displaces the regulatory proteins, activating the fiber. This action results in a possible strain-mediated depopulation of the SRX state of myosin and, thereby, attachment of more myosin heads to actin (Stewart et al., 2010).
evidence: The text cites a study showing ADP's effect on SRX state in skeletal muscle.

claim: Upon ADP treatment, increased SRX state turnover rates were observed in mouse psoas muscle fibers.
source: Similarly, upon ADP treatment, increased SRX state turnover rates were also observed in mouse psoas muscle fibers (Phung et al., 2018).
evidence: The text cites a study showing ADP's effect on SRX state turnover rates.

claim: ADP-mediated destabilization of the SRX population in cardiac tissue is affected to a lesser extent by rigor-ADP states than in skeletal fibers.
source: However, Hooijman et al., 2011 observed that such ADP-mediated destabilization of the SRX population in cardiac tissue is affected to a lesser extent by rigor-ADP states of adjacent myosin heads than is observed in skeletal fibers.
evidence: The text cites a study comparing ADP effects in cardiac vs skeletal tissue.

claim: In skeletal muscle at long sarcomere length without actin–myosin overlap, ADP did not alter the number of myosins in the SRX population but significantly increased the ATP turnover rates.
source: Very interestingly, in skeletal muscle, when the ADP-mediated dysregulation of the myosin SRX state was studied at long sarcomere length (without actin–myosin overlap), ADP did not alter the number of myosins in the SRX population but significantly increased the ATP turnover rates of these myosins, suggesting that binding of ADP to some myosin heads increases the rate of release of phosphate from adjacent heads (Stewart et al., 2010).
evidence: The text cites a study showing ADP's effect at long sarcomere length.

claim: ADP-mediated destabilization of the SRX population occurs in reconstituted porcine cardiac myosin thick filaments but not in S1 or HMM.
source: Recently, using porcine cardiac myosin, Gollapudi et al., 2020a have also shown an ADP-mediated destabilization of the SRX population of myosin in reconstituted myosin thick filaments, but not in the myosin subfragment S1 or heavy meromyosin (HMM), suggesting a relay mechanism of a cooperative destabilization of the SRX population, via the proximal and distal tails of myosin within the thick filament, which is absent in the shorter myosin constructs.
evidence: The text cites a study showing ADP effects in different myosin constructs.

claim: Higher temperature induces a higher proportion of myosin heads into the SRX state and slows the ATP turnover time in skeletal muscle.
source: For example, in skeletal muscle, higher temperature induces a higher proportion of myosin heads into the SRX state and slows the ATP turnover time for these myosins (Stewart et al., 2010), possibly by populating myosin in the pre-power stroke ADP.Pi state.
evidence: The text cites a study showing temperature effects on SRX state in skeletal muscle.

claim: In purified bovine cardiac myosin, with increasing temperature, the fraction of myosin in the SRX state decreased in S1 and had no effect in HMM.
source: However, in a purified bovine cardiac myosin system, Rohde et al., 2018 observed that with increasing temperature, the fraction of myosin in the SRX state decreased in an S1 system and had no effect in the HMM system, opposite of what was observed by the previous study of Stewart et al., 2010 in skeletal muscle fibers.
evidence: The text cites a study showing different temperature effects in cardiac myosin.

claim: Homozygous but not heterozygous MyBPC knockout mice have a significant decrease of the myosin population in the SRX state compared to WT.
source: It was first reported in a study with skinned cardiac muscle fibers that homozygous but not heterozygous MyBPC knockout mice have a significant decrease of the myosin population in the SRX state as compared to WT (McNamara et al., 2016).
evidence: The text cites a study showing MyBPC knockout effects on SRX state.

claim: The population of myosin in the SRX state increased in the presence of the C0-C7 MyBPC fragment in purified human β-cardiac myosin.
source: Consistent with this top-down observation, a bottom-up approach with purified human β-cardiac myosin recently demonstrated that the population of myosin in the SRX state increased in the presence of the C0-C7 MyBPC fragment (Sarkar et al., 2020).
evidence: The text cites a study showing MyBPC fragment effects on SRX state.

claim: In triple phosphomimetic version of cardiac MyBPC (DDD), the myosin SRX population significantly decreased compared to WT and triple phospho-ablated versions (AAA).
source: In another mouse study (McNamara et al., 2019), it was further shown that in a triple phosphomimetic version of cardiac MyBPC (DDD; serine→aspartate changes at residues 273, 282, and 302 of the M-domain of MyBPC), the myosin SRX population significantly decreased compared to WT and triple phospho-ablated versions of MyBPC (AAA; serine→alanine changes at residues 273, 282, and 302).
evidence: The text cites a study showing phosphomimetic MyBPC effects on SRX state.

claim: A phosphomimetic version of the ser 282 site (ADA) was sufficient to shift the DRX↔SRX state equilibrium toward the DRX state of myosin.
source: On further investigation of the site-specific phosphorylations, the authors showed that a phosphomimetic version of the ser 282 site (ADA; serine→aspartate change at residue 282, and serine→alanine changes at residues 273 and 302) was sufficient to shift the DRX↔SRX state equilibrium toward the DRX state of myosin.
evidence: The text describes findings about site-specific phosphorylation effects.

claim: The myosin ATPase lifetimes within the C-zone were significantly longer than those of the flanking non-MyBPC containing regions in rat soleus skeletal myofibrils.
source: The myosin ATPase lifetimes within the C-zone were significantly longer than those of the flanking non-MyBPC containing regions.
evidence: The text describes experimental findings about spatial differences in ATPase lifetimes.

claim: Within the C-zone, two different myosin populations corresponding to the DRX and SRX states were observed, while in non-MyBPC containing regions, all myosins were predominantly in the DRX state.
source: Also, within the C-zone, two different myosin populations corresponding to the DRX and SRX states were observed, while in the non-MyBPC containing regions, all myosins were predominantly in the DRX state, suggesting that the strongly inhibited SRX myosins exist predominantly within the C-zone of the skeletal sarcomere.
evidence: The text describes experimental findings about myosin state distributions in different sarcomere zones.

claim: The S1 head has been shown to interact with the proximal part of the S2 biochemically.
source: Furthermore, at a molecular level, the S1 head has been shown to interact with the proximal part of the S2 biochemically (Nag et al., 2017).
evidence: The text cites a study showing S1-S2 interactions.

claim: Human β-cardiac HMM containing the first 25 heptads of S2 (25-hep) showed significant stabilization of the myosin SRX population to ~60%.
source: One contained the first 25 heptads of the proximal part of the S2 subfragment (25-hep), and the other contained only the first two heptad repeats of the S2 subfragment (2-hep). In single turnover ATP experiments, the 25-hep HMM showed a significant stabilization of the myosin SRX population to ~60%.
evidence: The text describes experimental results comparing different HMM constructs.

claim: The SRX population in 2-hep HMM was ~20%.
source: In contrast, the SRX population in the 2-hep HMM was ~20%, suggesting that the proximal S2 sub-fragment of myosin shifts the myosin DRX↔SRX state equilibrium towards the SRX state.
evidence: The text describes experimental results for the 2-hep HMM construct.

claim: A high concentration of proximal S2 added to mouse ventricular cardiac muscle fibers significantly reduced the number of myosin heads in the SRX state.
source: In a different study, a high concentration of proximal S2 added to mouse ventricular cardiac muscle fibers significantly reduced the number of myosin heads in the SRX state (McNamara et al., 2019).
evidence: The text cites a study showing exogenous S2 effects on SRX state.

claim: Mutations in the MYH7 gene encoding β-cardiac myosin heavy chain are responsible for 20–30% of HCM cases.
source: Mutations in the MYH7 gene, which encodes the β-cardiac myosin heavy chain, are responsible for 20–30% of HCM cases (Ho et al., 2015).
evidence: The text cites a study on the genetic basis of HCM.

claim: HCM mutation hotspots consist of the myosin mesa, the converter domain, and the proximal-S2 tail region of myosin.
source: Homburger et al., 2016 demonstrated that these hotspots consist of a positively charged surface called the myosin mesa, the converter domain, and the proximal-S2 tail region of myosin.
evidence: The text cites a study identifying HCM mutation hotspots.

claim: Cardiac fibers from minipigs harboring the HCM-causing mutation R403Q demonstrated a depopulation of the SRX state.
source: Anderson et al., 2018 utilized cardiac fibers from minipigs harboring the HCM-causing mutation R403Q and demonstrated a depopulation of the SRX state by this mutation.
evidence: The text cites a study showing R403Q mutation effects on SRX state.

claim: Cardiac fibers from a human heart harboring the HCM-causing mutation R663H demonstrated SRX state depopulation.
source: Anderson et al., 2018 further demonstrated the SRX state depopulation in cardiac fibers from a human heart harboring another HCM-causing mutation, R663H.
evidence: The text cites a study showing R663H mutation effects on SRX state.

claim: Recombinant human β-cardiac myosin constructs harboring mutations in the myosin mesa (R249Q, H251N) and converter (D382Y, R719W) hotspots demonstrated depopulation of the SRX state.
source: A follow-up study by Adhikari et al., 2019 demonstrated the depopulation of the SRX state in recombinant human β-cardiac myosin constructs harboring mutations in the myosin mesa (R249Q, H251N) and converter (D382Y, R719W) hotspots of HCM mutations in myosin.
evidence: The text cites a study showing multiple HCM mutation effects on SRX state.

claim: Binding of cMyBPC fragment C0C7 populated the myosin SRX state in WT recombinant human β-cardiac myosin.
source: Interestingly, in an in vitro assay, binding of cMyBPC fragment C0C7 populated the myosin SRX state in WT recombinant human β-cardiac myosin.
evidence: The text describes experimental results showing MyBPC fragment effects.

claim: The HCM mutant R403Q myosin does not bind to C0C7, and hence its SRX state was not normalized.
source: However, the HCM mutant R403Q myosin, which dysregulates the myosin SRX state, does not bind to C0C7, and hence its SRX state was not normalized.
evidence: The text describes experimental results for R403Q mutant myosin.

claim: The R663H HCM-causing myosin, which does bind C0C7, did not show any induction of the SRX state.
source: Interestingly, the R663H HCM-causing myosin, which does bind C0C7, also did not show any induction of the SRX state (Sarkar et al., 2020).
evidence: The text cites a study showing R663H mutant myosin behavior with MyBPC.

claim: Mouse cardiac left ventricular tissue harboring R403Q, V606M, and R719W mutations demonstrated depopulation of the SRX state.
source: Reconfirming observations by Anderson et al., 2018 and Adhikari et al., 2019, most recently, Toepfer et al., 2020 measured the SRX state in mouse cardiac left ventricular tissue (predominantly MYH6 – α-cardiac myosin) harboring R403Q, V606M, and R719W mutations and demonstrated depopulation of the SRX state in these samples.
evidence: The text cites a study showing multiple HCM mutation effects in mouse tissue.

claim: Human iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes harboring HCM mutations showed significant depopulation of the SRX state.
source: In the same study, they introduced these mutations in human induced pluripotent stem cell -derived cardiomyocytes and observed a similar significant depopulation of the SRX state in this cell-based assay.
evidence: The text describes experimental results in iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes.

claim: HCM reflects a loss of function of the SRX state.
source: The effect of mutations in myosin that increase activity by inhibiting the SRX state explains the puzzling observation that HCM, which is an apparent gain of function, is more prevalent than DCM, an apparent loss of function. In general, gain-of-function mutations are rare. HCM reflects a loss of function of the SRX state.
evidence: The text presents an interpretation of HCM as a loss of SRX state function.

claim: Fluorescent probes attached to cysteine residues in the EF hand region of RLC showed the greatest depopulation of the SRX state.
source: Probes attached to cysteine residues in a region called the EF hand, which coordinates divalent cations like Mg2+ or Ca2+ on the RLC, showed the greatest depopulation of the SRX state.
evidence: The text describes experimental results with fluorescent probes on RLC.

claim: The HCM-causing R58Q mutation in RLC populates the SRX state to a greater extent than WT in reconstituted porcine fibers and transgenic mouse papillary muscle samples.
source: A follow-up study by Yadav et al., 2019 demonstrated that, contrary to the widely held hypothesis that HCM mutations shift myosin to the DRX state, the HCM-causing R58Q mutation populates the SRX state in reconstituted porcine fibers and transgenic mouse papillary muscle samples to an even greater extent than WT.
evidence: The text cites a study showing R58Q mutation effects on SRX state.

claim: A phosphomimetic mutation S15D in the R58Q background rescued the R58Q-induced adverse effects in reconstituted porcine fibers.
source: A phosphomimetic mutation S15D, when introduced in the R58Q background, was demonstrated to rescue the R58Q-induced adverse effects in reconstituted porcine fibers.
evidence: The text describes experimental results showing rescue effects of S15D mutation.

claim: The ELC mutation A57G in an ELC-humanized mouse model of HCM significantly depopulated the SRX state.
source: In this study, they studied the effect of the ELC mutation A57G in an ELC-humanized mouse model of HCM. SRX state was significantly depopulated in these mice, but there were no significant changes in the lifetimes of the SRX or DRX states.
evidence: The text describes experimental results for A57G ELC mutation.

claim: Truncation or missense mutations in the cardiac MyBPC gene are responsible for ~30–40% of HCM cases.
source: Truncation or missense mutations in the cardiac MyBPC gene are responsible for ~30–40% of HCM cases (Ho et al., 2015).
evidence: The text cites a study on MyBPC mutations in HCM.

claim: Homozygous cMyBPC knockout mouse hearts had significantly higher heart weight to body weight ratio than WT.
source: The heart weight to body weight ratio of the homozygous knockout mouse was significantly higher than the WT mouse.
evidence: The text describes experimental results comparing knockout and WT mice.

claim: Homozygous cMyBPC knockout fibers showed significant depopulation of the SRX state while heterozygous fibers showed similar SRX state values compared to WT.
source: Upon performing SRX state assays with isolated cardiac fibers from these animals, the authors discovered a significant depopulation of the SRX state in the homozygous fibers. In contrast, the heterozygous fibers showed similar SRX state values compared to the WT.
evidence: The text describes experimental results for MyBPC knockout effects.

claim: Human HCM samples harboring missense or truncation MyBPC mutations had significantly depopulated SRX state combined with decreased rate of ATP turnover by myosin in the SRX state compared to non-failing donor hearts.
source: They discovered that compared to the non-failing hearts, the samples harboring missense or truncation MyBPC mutations had a significantly depopulated the SRX state combined with a decreased rate of ATP turnover by myosin in the SRX state.
evidence: The text describes experimental results from human HCM samples.

claim: A graded loss of cMyBPC results in a subsequent graded loss of the SRX state.
source: Recently, Toepfer et al., 2019 demonstrated that a graded loss of cMyBPC results in a subsequent graded loss of the SRX state.
evidence: The text cites a study showing dose-dependent MyBPC effects on SRX state.

claim: Heterozygous cMyBPC truncating mutation fibers had a 50% decrease in the SRX state compared to a 94% decrease in homozygous fibers.
source: The heterozygous fibers had a 50% decrease in the SRX state compared to a 94% decrease in the homozygous fibers.
evidence: The text describes quantitative experimental results for MyBPC mutations.

claim: Skinned human HCM heart fibers with heterozygous cMyBPC truncations showed ~50% decrease in the SRX population compared to WT human fibers.
source: In this study, they also measured the SRX state in skinned human HCM heart fibers with heterozygous cMyBPC truncations. Once again, they observed a ~50% decrease in the SRX population of these mutant fibers compared to the WT human fibers.
evidence: The text describes experimental results from human HCM fibers.

claim: Omecamtiv mecarbil (OM) is a cardiac sarcomere activator that completed phase III trials to treat systolic heart failure.
source: The first clinical candidate identified for direct targeting of cardiac myosin was Cytokinetics' omecamtiv mecarbil (OM) (Malik et al., 2011), a cardiac sarcomere activator that currently completed phase III trials to treat systolic heart failure.
evidence: The text cites information about OM's clinical development status.

claim: Mavacamten is a small-molecule inhibitor of β-cardiac myosin in phase III trials to treat obstructive HCM.
source: MyoKardia's mavacamten (previously MYK-461) is a small-molecule inhibitor of β-cardiac myosin (Green et al., 2016) and is in phase III trials to treat obstructive HCM.
evidence: The text cites information about mavacamten's clinical development status.

claim: OM has been shown to inhibit the basal ATPase activity of cardiac myosin.
source: However, OM has been shown to inhibit the basal ATPase activity of cardiac myosin (Malik et al., 2011), which hints that it might also induce the SRX state in this system.
evidence: The text cites a study showing OM's effect on myosin ATPase.

claim: The crystal structure of OM-bound bovine cardiac myosin shows that OM binds to a 'pre-powerstroke' pocket of the myosin.
source: The crystal structure of OM-bound bovine cardiac myosin has been published, showing that OM binds to a 'pre-powerstroke' pocket of the myosin (Planelles-Herrero et al., 2017).
evidence: The text cites a structural study of OM-bound myosin.

claim: Mavacamten was discovered as an ATPase inhibitor that inhibits phosphate release from the enzymatic pocket of cardiac myosin.
source: Mavacamten was discovered as an ATPase inhibitor that inhibits phosphate release, specifically from the enzymatic pocket of cardiac myosin (Green et al., 2016).
evidence: The text cites the discovery study of mavacamten's mechanism.

claim: Mavacamten treatment brought the SRX state levels of R403Q and R663H mutant fibers back to WT values of 30–40%.
source: Later, Anderson et al., 2018, who demonstrated a depopulation of the SRX state in minipig cardiac fibers harboring the R403Q mutation and in human cardiac fibers with the R663H mutation, showed a re-population of the SRX state when these mutant fibers were treated with mavacamten. Treatment with mavacamten brought the SRX state levels of the mutant fibers back to WT values of 30–40%.
evidence: The text cites a study showing mavacamten's rescue effect on mutant fibers.

claim: Mavacamten increased helical ordering of WT and mutant thick filaments as demonstrated by X-ray diffraction.
source: By utilizing X-ray diffraction, the authors demonstrated an increase in helical ordering of the WT and mutant thick filaments with mavacamten.
evidence: The text describes structural evidence for mavacamten's effects.

claim: Single-particle negative-staining electron microscopy demonstrated that mavacamten stabilized a compact state of myosin in which the heads were folded back against the tail.
source: Single-particle negative-staining electron microscopy demonstrated that mavacamten stabilized a compact state of myosin in which the heads were folded back against the tail.
evidence: The text describes structural evidence for mavacamten's effects on myosin conformation.

claim: Mavacamten could induce a partial SRX population in shorter myosin constructs that lack the tail region.
source: In the same study, the authors also demonstrated that enzymatically, mavacamten could induce a partial SRX population in shorter myosin constructs that lack the tail region.
evidence: The text describes experimental results showing mavacamten effects in different myosin constructs.

claim: The potency of mavacamten to populate the SRX state is highest in reconstituted myosin thick filaments and least in S1.
source: In harmony with these observations, by looking at a dose-response of mavacamten, Gollapudi et al., 2020a observed that its potency to populate the SRX state of myosin is the highest in reconstituted myosin thick filaments and least in S1.
evidence: The text cites a study showing dose-response effects of mavacamten.

claim: The efficacy of mavacamten is similar in WT and mutant R403Q ventricular β-cardiac and WT atrial α-cardiac myosin.
source: In the same study, they show that the efficacy of mavacamten is similar in WT and mutant R403Q ventricular β-cardiac and WT atrial α-cardiac myosin (Gollapudi et al., 2020a).
evidence: The text cites a study comparing mavacamten efficacy across myosin types.

claim: The effect of mavacamten to populate the myosin SRX state was diminished in the presence of ADP.
source: They extended their study by showing that the effect of mavacamten to populate the myosin SRX state was diminished in the presence of ADP, consistent with the activation mechanism detailed above for the ADP-bound myosin heads
evidence: The text describes experimental results showing ADP's effect on mavacamten action.

claim: Mavacamten treatment reverted the depopulation of the SRX state caused by truncating mutations in MyBPC in mouse cardiac samples.
source: Toepfer et al., 2019 demonstrated that truncating mutations in MyBPC depopulated the SRX state in mouse cardiac samples (see section 'HCM-causing mutations in MyBPC also dysregulate the myosin SRX state'), and this depopulation was reverted when the fibers were treated with mavacamten.
evidence: The text cites a study showing mavacamten's rescue effect on MyBPC mutant fibers.

claim: Mavacamten treatment doubled myosin in the SRX state in the D- and P-zones of slow skeletal myofibrils while the SRX population of C-zone myosin remained relatively the same.
source: They treated the myofibrils with mavacamten and observed a doubling of myosin in the SRX state in the D- and P-zones. In contrast, the SRX population of C-zone myosin remained relatively the same.
evidence: The text describes experimental results showing spatial effects of mavacamten.

claim: Blebbistatin is a widely used ATPase inhibitor of myosin-II that binds inside the 50 kDa cleft of myosin and prevents the cleft from closing.
source: Another tool compound, blebbistatin, is a widely used ATPase inhibitor of myosin-II. Blebbistatin binds inside the 50 kDa cleft of myosin and prevents the cleft from closing (Allingham et al., 2005).
evidence: The text cites a study describing blebbistatin's mechanism of action.

claim: Blebbistatin caused inhibition of nucleotide turnover in both fast and slow skeletal muscle fibers with a large component (~40%) decaying at a prolonged rate with a time constant of ~3600 s.
source: Wilson et al., 2014 demonstrated that blebbistatin caused inhibition of nucleotide turnover in both fast and slow skeletal muscle fibers. They observed a large component of the signal (~40%) decayed at a prolonged rate with a time constant of ~3600 s.
evidence: The text cites a study showing blebbistatin's effects on nucleotide turnover.

claim: Blebbistatin did not change the population of molecules in the SRX state but observed a net decrease in the ATPase rate of the SRX population.
source: They did not observe a change in the population of molecules in the SRX state, but they observed a net decrease in the ATPase rate of the SRX population.
evidence: The text describes experimental results for blebbistatin's effects on SRX state.

claim: Blebbistatin or its derivatives like para-nitro or para-amino blebbistatin have no impact on the SRX population of bovine cardiac reconstituted thick filaments.
source: A recent study by Gollapudi et al. demonstrated no impact of blebbistatin or its derivatives like para-nitro or para-amino blebbistatin on the SRX population of bovine cardiac reconstitutedthick filaments (Gollapudi et al., 2020b; Gollapudi et al., 2020c).
evidence: The text cites studies showing blebbistatin's lack of effect on SRX population.

claim: Piperine is the primary alkaloid component of black pepper, isolated from Piper nigrum.
source: Piperine is the primary alkaloid component of black pepper, isolated from an Indian medicinal plant, Piper nigrum.
evidence: The text states the source and nature of piperine.

claim: Piperine can mitigate obesity and type 2 diabetes in rodent models.
source: Previous studies have shown that piperine can also mitigate obesity and type 2 diabetes in rodent models (Nogara et al., 2016b; BrahmaNaidu et al., 2014; Choi et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: The text cites studies showing piperine's effects in rodent models.

claim: Piperine depopulated the SRX state in fast-twitch skeletal fibers, but not in slow-twitch skeletal or cardiac fibers.
source: Nogara et al., 2016b demonstrated that piperine depopulated the SRX state in fast-twitch skeletal fibers, but not in slow-twitch skeletal or cardiac fibers.
evidence: The text cites a study showing piperine's selective effects on different muscle types.

claim: Piperine increased the ATPase activity of relaxed skinned fibers by ~66%.
source: It increased the ATPase activity of relaxed skinned fibers by ~66%.
evidence: The text describes quantitative experimental results for piperine's effects.

claim: Piperine binds the HMM fragment of myosin, but not the S1-fragment which lacks the RLC.
source: In follow-up work, Tolkatchev et al., 2018 discovered that piperine binds the heavy meromyosin (HMM) fragment of myosin, but not the S1-fragment, which lacks the RLC.
evidence: The text cites a study showing piperine's binding specificity.

claim: Shifting heads out of the SRX state into the DRX state would increase the whole-body metabolic rate in humans by 500 kcal/day.
source: The authors estimate that shifting heads out of the SRX state into the DRX state would increase the whole-body metabolic rate in humans by 500 kcal/day.
evidence: The text presents an estimate of metabolic effects.

claim: Administration of piperine depopulated the myosin SRX state in human skeletal myosin obtained from biopsies of lean and obese subjects, without affecting human cardiac cells.
source: Recently Wilson et al., 2021 showed that administration of piperine depopulated the myosin SRX state in human skeletal myosin obtained from biopsies of lean and obsese subjects, without affecting the human cardiac cells.
evidence: The text cites a study showing piperine's effects in human tissue samples.

claim: The fraction of myosin heads in the SRX state increased systematically as the ionic strength decreased in long-tailed 25-hep HMM myosin.
source: Anderson et al., 2018 studied the ionic strength dependence on the SRX state of long-tailed 25-hep HMM myosin, and they observed that the fraction of myosin heads in the SRX state increased systematically as the ionic strength decreased.
evidence: The text cites a study showing ionic strength effects on SRX state.

claim: Ionic strength effects on SRX state were not seen in either the short-tailed 2-hep HMM or the sS1 version of myosin.
source: This observation was not seen in either the short-tailed 2-hep HMM or the sS1 (S1 without the RLC) version of the myosin.
evidence: The text describes experimental results showing construct-specific ionic strength effects.

claim: In the presence of actin, the amplitude of the SRX population decreased and the ATP turnover rates of myosins in the SRX state increased for bovine cardiac HMM.
source: For example, for the bovine cardiac HMM, the amplitude of the SRX population decreased, and the ATP turnover rates of these myosins in the SRX state increased in the presence of actin, suggesting an overall shift of the myosins toward a DRX-like state.
evidence: The text cites experimental results showing actin's effects on SRX state.

claim: Mavacamten could only populate ~50% of HMM in the SRX state in the presence of actin, compared to ~90% without actin.
source: Moreover, mavacamten, which otherwise populated ~90% of the HMM in the SRX state (as described in the 'Mavacamten' section), could only do so to ~50% in the presence of actin.
evidence: The text describes experimental results showing actin's effect on mavacamten action.

claim: Smaller sub-fragments of cardiac myosins such as S1 and 2-hep HMM that are incompetent to achieve the folded-back IHM structure still exhibit SRX state properties.
source: As discussed earlier, it has been shown in multiple studies that the smaller sub-fragments of cardiac myosins, such as S1 and 2-hep HMM, that are incompetent to achieve the folded-back IHM structure, still exhibit SRX state properties (Anderson et al., 2018; Gollapudi et al., 2020a; Rohde et al., 2018).
evidence: The text cites multiple studies showing SRX state in non-IHM-forming constructs.

claim: The SRX state of myosin is a functional outcome of a different conformation of the myosin lever arm.
source: With this knowledge combined with homology models of the IHM state, it has been argued that the SRX state of myosin is a functional outcome of a different conformation of the myosin lever arm (Anderson et al., 2018; Spudich, 2019).
evidence: The text cites studies proposing lever arm conformation as the basis for SRX state.

claim: A conformation in which the lever arm is tilted more in the pre-stroke direction could give rise to a low-energy consuming state that may resemble the SRX state.
source: More precisely, it has been reasoned that a conformation in which the lever arm is tilted more in the pre-stroke direction could give rise to a low-energy consuming state that may resemble the SRX state (Anderson et al., 2018; Spudich, 2019).
evidence: The text cites studies proposing a specific lever arm conformation for SRX state.

claim: OM decreases the thick-filament order and helical symmetry and stabilizes the structural 'on' state in which myosin heads are more perpendicular to the axis of the thick filament.
source: However, two different structural studies, one using fluorescence polarization spectroscopy by Kampourakis et al., 2018 and the other using X-ray fiber diffraction studies of intact rat cardiac fibers by Caremani et al., 2020, have suggested that OM decreases the thick-filament order and helical symmetry and stabilizes the structural 'on' state in which myosin heads are more perpendicular to the axis of the thick filament.
evidence: The text cites structural studies showing OM's effects on thick filament structure.

claim: Blebbistatin promotes an IHM-like compact folded-back structure and helical ordering in both isolated purified myosins and skeletal muscle fibers.
source: Likewise, it is known from multiple structural studies that blebbistatin promotes an IHM-like compact folded-back structure and helical ordering in both isolated purified myosins and skeletal muscle fibers (Zhao et al., 2008; Xu et al., 2009).
evidence: The text cites structural studies showing blebbistatin's effects on myosin structure.

claim: Recent small-angle X-ray scattering data suggests that blebbistatin locks myosin into a single conformation between the classic open and the folded IHM states.
source: Supportive of this notion, recent small-angle X-ray scattering data suggests that blebbistatin locks myosin into a single conformation between the classic open and the folded IHM states (Gollapudi et al., 2020c).
evidence: The text cites a structural study showing blebbistatin's effect on myosin conformation.

claim: Using cryo-electron microscopy, the folded back IHM structure of smooth muscle myosin at ~4–8 Å resolution was independently determined in two studies.
source: Very recently, using cryo-electron microscopy, two subsequent seminal works have determined the folded-back IHM structure of smooth muscle myosin at ~4–8 Å resolution (Scarff et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: The text cites two recent cryo-EM studies of smooth muscle myosin IHM structure.

claim: In the smooth muscle myosin IHM structure, the 'blocked head' appears to have its lever arm primed more in the pre-stroke conformation compared to the 'free head'.
source: Very recently, using cryo-electron microscopy, the folded back IHM structure of smooth muscle myosin at ~4–8 Å resolution was independently determined in two studies, demonstrating that the 'blocked head' appears to have its lever arm primed more in the pre-stroke conformation as compared to the 'free head'.
evidence: The text describes structural findings from cryo-EM studies.
